meeting_header: Date/Time: 2025-11-20 15:00 PST | Duration: 62 mins | Redwood: Jesse Porter, Samir Patel, Maya Lin | Northshore Bank: Priya Singh (CISO), Tom Wallace (Head of Cloud), Evan Morris (DevOps), Sofia Alvarez (Compliance)
summary: Deep dive on Private/VPC deployment architecture for Northshore Bank. Covered network isolation, ingress/egress patterns, firewalling, peering vs transit, KMS/HSM key management, audit logs and retention, RBAC/SSO integration, and compliance artifacts (SOC 2 / ISO). Identified follow-ups: send SOC2 docs, share VPC peering and firewall recommendations, schedule workshop, gather customer firewall constraints.
transcript:
[00:00] Jesse (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you carving out time. We wanted to run through the private VPC architecture and answer detailed network and compliance questions. Quick roll call?
[00:14] Priya (Northshore - CISO): Hi this is Priya, CISO. We have Tom, our head of cloud, Evan from DevOps and Sofia from compliance on.
[00:22] Tom: Yup, Tom here.
[00:24] Evan: Evan, hi.
[00:26] Jesse: Great. Samir from our SE team will lead the topology discussion. Samir over to you.
[00:34] Samir (Redwood SE): Thanks. So high-level, our Private offering runs a customer-dedicated control plane with a customer-managed VPC peering or private link depending on your cloud. You can choose VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink, or an on-prem connector for air-gapped setups. The key areas customers ask about are ingress/egress egress controls, how we do firewalling, and where keys/logs live.
[00:58] Priya: Let's start with network isolation. We have strict segmentation requirements; production models must not have the ability to egress to internet by default. How does Redwood prevent accidental egress?
[01:10] Samir: By default we recommend a one-way egress model only to the minimum required endpoints. For hosted control plane options we propose VPC peering with route tables that only allow outbound to Redwood-managed endpoints over specific ports. For full air-gapped we support a private on-prem agent that never touches public internet.
[01:30] Evan: When you say "endpoints" do you mean S3 or your registry? We store models in our S3 and want to know if data paths go outside.
[01:38] Maya (Redwood): Good question — for private deployments, model artifacts can remain in your S3 (via VPC endpoints or S3 gateway); we don't pull artifacts through public internet. We also offer an option to mirror models into a private registry inside your VPC.
[01:55] Tom: Network address translation — does Redwood require NAT gateways on our side for egress, or do you recommend provisioning dedicated NAT?
[02:04] Samir: We usually recommend controlled NAT or use of egress-only interfaces with strict security groups. In AWS setups customers often provide a NAT gateway in a dedicated egress subnet, then we restrict routes so only traffic to specific Redwood IPs is allowed. We can also support AWS PrivateLink which avoids NAT entirely. There's a tradeoff: PrivateLink is more lock-in and has per-endpoint costs, peering is simpler but requires route table discipline.
[02:30] Priya: For compliance, auditability is critical. How do you surface audit logs and what is the retention?
[02:38] Jesse: We ship audit logs from the control plane and runtime — we can push to your SIEM via Kinesis/Firehose, CloudWatch subscriptions, or Splunk HTTP intake. Standard retention on our side is 90 days, but for Private you can configure logs to stream directly to your storage and manage retention to meet SOC 2/ISO requirements.
[02:58] Sofia: And are logs tamper-evident? We need to ensure immutability for certain records.
[03:04] Samir: For sensitive customers we recommend writing logs to an append-only store you control (S3 with Object Lock) and we support log signing options. On-prem HSM-backed signing of audit records is available in air-gapped deployments.
[03:20] Priya: Encryption and key management — we need BYOK and HSM backed keys, key rotation, and separation of duties.
[03:28] Maya: We support KMS integrations — customer-managed keys in AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or HSM via Cloud HSM. For on-prem we integrate with external HSMs over PKCS#11 and can do BYOK with hardware-backed keys. Key rotation policies are compatible with Azure/AWS/FIPS controls.
[03:48] Evan: Can you confirm whether ephemeral encryption keys are used for in-memory model inference and whether any secret material leaves our VPC?
[03:55] Samir: No secret material leaves your VPC unencrypted. We use ephemeral session keys for transport-level encryption and the data plane runs in your environment for private deployments, so keys are only referenced by the runtime. For hosted variants we encrypt at rest and in transit; customer KMS can be used so Redwood never has plaintext access.
[04:16] Tom: What about RBAC and SSO? Our enterprise uses SAML + SCIM provisioning and we need fine-grained role controls for model access and deployment.
[04:26] Jesse: We support SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning, and can integrate with your IdP. Role-based access can be mapped to your groups, and we expose audit records for admin actions and model rollouts. For Private customers, RBAC enforcement is controlled locally in your control plane and logs are streamed out.
[04:47] Priya: Any certifications you can share? SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001?
[04:52] Jesse: Yes — Redwood maintains SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 artifacts for our hosted controls; for Private deployments we provide a shared responsibility matrix and can provide a SOC 2 bridge letter plus controls mapping. We'll follow up with the actual reports.
[05:06] Sofia: Data residency — we need all inference data processed in-region. How do you guarantee region locality?
[05:14] Samir: For Private VPC deployments we run the runtime inside your region and you control the compute. For hosted Dedicated we can pin capacity to specific regions; for private you can choose the region and we don't route data elsewhere. We'll provide topology diagrams showing region boundaries and peering.
[05:33] Evan: Firewalling detail — can you provide the exact port ranges, IPs, and whether you support TLS inspection break-glass?
[05:41] Samir: We'll provide a whitelist of IPs and FQDNs used by the control plane. Ports are typical HTTPS 443 for control plane, gRPC/tcp for runtime communications can be pinned to narrow ranges. We recommend avoiding TLS inspection on control plane traffic because it interferes with mTLS and client certs. If you do TLS inspection, we advise an allowlist for mTLS endpoints and separate monitoring.
[06:04] Priya: mTLS — is mutual TLS supported for runtime-to-control-plane connections?
[06:09] Samir: Yes. For the private connector we use mTLS; certificate management can be integrated with your PKI. We also support client certificates issued by your CA.
[06:20] Tom: How does model rollback and canary deploys happen inside our VPC? We need audit trail that shows who deployed which model version.
[06:29] Maya: Rollouts are controlled by the management plane; for Private we give you the control plane so those actions are logged locally and you can configure canary percentages. Each deployment event includes user id, timestamp and model hash in the audit log so you can verify immutability.
[06:45] Evan: About egress — if the runtime needs to pull from external repos, can we restrict to mirror-only?
[06:51] Samir: Absolutely. We recommend mirroring models into your private registry and blocking public repos at the firewall. That avoids runtime needing to egress to public endpoints.
[07:02] Priya: Any special consideration for KV cache or attention cache? I heard some talk about KV cache in Redwood docs.
[07:09] Samir: The KV cache lives with the runtime; in private setups it stays within your VPC. There was a docs typo once calling it "K-V cash" in a slide, so sorry about that — but it's stored in ephemeral memory and optionally persisted to your managed storage if you enable cache warm starts, in which case those persisted segments inherit your storage encryption policies.
[07:33] Jesse: Ok lets surface the main risk areas: network misconfiguration, key management, and log retention. For network misconfig we recommend a hardened reference terraform module we'll share.
[07:44] Tom: Would love that. Also any recommended firewall rules for blocked outbound ranges?
[07:49] Samir: We'll include a recommended deny-by-default baseline, then explicit allows to Redwood control plane IPs and your S3 endpoints. We'll share CIDR ranges and hostedcontrolplane FQDNs.
[08:00] Sofia: Legal will need a data processing addendum and proof of encryption in transit and at rest.
[08:06] Jesse: We'll attach our DPA template and summary of encryption controls.
[08:11] Priya: For audits, will your team participate in our SOC 2 readiness and answer control questions?
[08:18] Jesse: Yes, Redwood security will respond to questionnaires and provide evidence for our managed controls. For Private deployments the boundary shifts and we'll document which controls are customer-owned.
[08:29] Evan: Any constraints on metrics we can ship to our monitoring? We want token-level latency breakdowns into our Datadog.
[08:36] Maya: You can forward telemetry via StatsD/Prometheus or push metrics to Datadog via our exporter. For private we can expose Prometheus endpoints inside your VPC.
[08:47] Tom: Let's talk uptime guarantees. What SLAs do you offer for private deployments?
[08:52] Jesse: For Dedicated we offer SLA-backed uptime; for Private it's contractible — we typically set targets and runbooks as part of the enterprise agreement. We'll provide an SLA proposal in the next deck.
[09:06] Priya: A couple of nitty-gritty items — how do you handle software patching in air-gapped environments?
[09:12] Samir: For on-prem we provide appliance images you ingest on your offline repo. We support signed update bundles that you can validate with your chain. We can also run an operator in your cluster to handle upgrades with canary approaches.
[09:28] Evan: If we use your private connector, what outbound DNS calls happen? We need to block any unexpected external DNS.
[09:36] Samir: We'll supply a DNS allowlist. Most control plane egress is to our FQDNs on port 443; we recommend forcing DNS resolution via internal resolvers and locking down external DNS.
[09:47] Priya: Anything else on compliance? Data residency, right to be forgotten concerns?
[09:53] Jesse: For private the data is in your environment and you control retention. For hosted options we offer deletion APIs and data retention controls. We'll include the deletion certification process for PII.
[10:04] Tom: Ok team, next steps?
[10:07] Jesse: Quick recap — we'll send SOC2/ISO artifacts, share the VPC peering and firewall templates, schedule the 90-min architecture workshop, and produce POC pricing. Anything to add?
[10:19] Priya: Please include the list of exact IPs and port ranges in the template.
[10:23] Sofia: And the DPA.
[10:25] Jesse: Got it. Thanks everyone.
[10:28] [Meeting ends]
